articles.description:
Part 3 of a series on building reliable AI systems
In Part 1, we explored why testing AI systems is different.
Now let’s focus on one of the most widely used (and misunderstood) patterns:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
RAG is often seen as a solution to hallucinations.
In reality, it just shifts the problem.
A typical RAG pipeline looks like this:
User Query
    ↓
Retriever → Context
    ↓
LLM → Response

When something goes wrong, it’s not always obvious where the failure is.
Did retrieval fail?
Was the context irrelevant?
Did the model ignore the context?
Or did it hallucinate anyway?
Without proper evaluation, everything looks like a “model problem.”
This is the key insight:
You are not evaluating a single system—you are evaluating two tightly coupled systems.

articles.title: Evaluating RAG Systems: Measuring Retrieval Quality, Grounding, and Hallucinations

articles.author: zvone187
articles.description:
If your recurring agent task keeps dying seconds before it posts results, the bootstrap is eating your timeout. A richly configured agent burns 60 to 120 seconds on memory loading, credentials, and skill discovery before it ever makes its first tool call. Everything after that competes for what's left of the budget, and the last step, usually the Slack post or email your team actually sees, is the one that gets clipped.
Size your timeout as bootstrap_p95 + work_p95 + buffer, not just the work. Bootstrap (memory loading, credentials scan, skill discovery) commonly costs 60 to 120 seconds on a richly configured agent before the first tool call fires. That means your effective budget is smaller than whatever you typed into the config. Then reorder so the human-facing output runs before cleanu…
articles.title: Why Your Recurring Agent Task Dies Right Before Delivery

articles.author: Ender Ahmet Yurt
articles.description:
I love Ruby. I love the console. I do not love this:
{:name=>"Alice", :score=>100, :active=>true}
{:name=>"Bob", :score=>42, :active=>false}

When you have 20 of these in a row, good luck reading anything.
So I built a tiny gem called typed_print.
One thing. Just one.
It turns hashes into clean, aligned tables.
require 'typed_print'

data = [
  { name: "Alice", score: 100, active: true },
  { name: "Bob", score: 42, active: false }
]

TypedPrint.print(data)

Output
 Name  Score Active 
------+------+-------
Alice   100 true   
Bob      42 false  

That's it. No magic. No mental parsing.
pp is fine, but still hard to scan.
awesome_print is great, but sometimes you don't want colors, JSON support, or 10 dependencies.
I wanted something that:
Has zero required dependencies
Only does tables
Wo…

articles.author: Alex Kamnier Crypto Arbitrage & AI Developer
articles.description:
The 2026 crypto landscape is more fragmented than ever. With liquidity split between TON, Solana, and EVM L2s, the real challenge for developers isn't just trading—it's synchronized data monitoring.
In this post, I want to break down the logic of high-speed liquidity tracking and how to handle latency spikes when monitoring DEX pools like STON.fi or Jupiter.
The Latency Challenge
Basic Monitoring Snippet (Python)
`Python
import asyncio
import time

class LiquidityMonitor:
    def __init__(self, chain_id, rpc_url):
        self.chain_id = chain_id
        self.rpc = rpc_url
        self.latency_threshold = 0.05  # 50ms target

    async def fetch_pool_data(self):
        # Logic for real-time price fetching
        start_time = time.perf_counter()
        # Simulation of an RPC call
        await asyncio.sleep(0.02) 
        end_time = time.perf_counter()

        execution_time = end_time - start_time
        if execution_time > self.latency_threshold:
            print(f"[{self.chain_id}] Warning: Latency spike detected: {execution_time:.4f}s")
        return execution_time

async def main():
    monitor = LiquidityMonitor("Solana", "https://api.mainnet-beta.solana.com")
    await monitor.fetch_pool_data()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())`

Why MEV Protection Matters
Conclusion
You can find the technical documentation and the full source code by searching for "Cortex AI crypto arbitrage bot" on GitHub or Google. I'd love to hear your thoughts on handling TON network latency in the comments!
articles.title: Solving Liquidity Fragmentation: Building a Cross-Chain Monitoring Engine in Python 2026
